clinicalPearls: A functional defecation disorder in which impaired coordination of the abdominal, rectal and pelvic floor muscles prevents effective evacuation
Patients strain excessively, feel incomplete evacuation and may use digital manoeuvres to pass stool
There is paradoxical contraction or inadequate relaxation of the anal sphincter and pelvic floor during attempted defecation, or inadequate propulsive force
It is a common and often overlooked cause of refractory constipation
Diagnosis requires anorectal physiology testing, including manometry and a balloon expulsion test
Biofeedback-based pelvic floor retraining is the treatment of choice and is more effective than laxatives alone
reference.pathophysiology: Dyssynergic defecation is a disorder of the coordinated neuromuscular sequence required for normal evacuation. Rather than the normal rise in rectal pressure with relaxation of the anal sphincter and pelvic floor, affected patients show paradoxical pelvic floor and sphincter contraction, incomplete relaxation, or insufficient rectal propulsive force. This learned incoordination obstructs stool passage despite otherwise normal colonic function, and because it is a behavioural motor-control problem it responds to retraining rather than to laxatives targeting transit.
additionalInvestigations: Anorectal manometry to demonstrate the dyssynergic pattern
Defecography where structural outlet problems are suspected
Colonic transit study to assess for coexisting slow transit
Digital rectal examination as an initial screen for impaired relaxation
redFlags: Suspected structural outlet obstruction requiring surgery
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is good, with the majority improving through biofeedback-directed pelvic floor retraining; outcomes are poorer if the diagnosis is missed and only laxatives are used.
pitfalls: Treating refractory constipation with escalating laxatives without testing for dyssynergia
Overlooking the diagnosis on a normal-appearing colon
Missing a coexisting structural outlet problem
Not referring for biofeedback, the definitive treatment
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
